title: When Sounds Hurt and Voices Aren’t Heard: An Experience Report on Misophonia, Sensory Trauma, and Trauma-Informed Design

paper.title: When Sounds Hurt and Voices Aren’t Heard: An Experience Report on Misophonia, Sensory Trauma, and Trauma-Informed Design
paper.abstract: Abstract. This experience report reflects on researching misophonia as someone who lives with it. Misophonia is an aversive response to everyday sounds (chewing, sniffling, pen clicking) and, for many of us, to associated visual cues (misokinesia). It is poorly recognized clinically and socially. People with misophonia are routinely disbelieved, and they live inside platform surfaces (auto-playing audio, algorithmic ASMR, normalized eating on camera) that turn the sensory environment itself into recurring distress. This report is a re-reading of a prior qualitative study of 16 semi-structured interviews with misophones ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) , conducted in dialogue with my lived experience and my role in the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network. I extend the trauma-informed design (TID) conversation ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) in two ways. First, TID must treat embodied, contested conditions as sources of both sensory and epistemic harm: ongoing trauma produced by the audiovisual surface and by repeated dismissal of users’ accounts of their bodies. Second, the closed groups and moderated subreddits participants relied on can reproduce that dismissal when a few moderators decide whose experiences count. I close with implications for ASSETS.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction and Positionality
sections.text: I write this report as someone who lives with misophonia and as a researcher who studies how design can support people whose experiences are routinely disbelieved. Misophonia is an aversive, often involuntary response to specific everyday sounds (chewing, slurping, sniffling, tongue clicking, pen clicking, keyboard typing, joint cracking) and, for many of us, to the visual cues that accompany them, a co-occurring sensitivity sometimes called misokinesia ( Jaswal et al., 2021 ) . Recent consensus work defines misophonia as a distinct disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds ( Swedo et al., 2022 ) , but it has no DSM entry and no settled clinical home ( Cavanna and Seri, 2015 ; Schröder et al., 2013 ; Taylor, 2017 ; Potgieter et al., 2019 ) . People who live with it spend extraordinary effort just to be believed , and, in parallel, extraordinary effort to make ordinary platform surfaces survivable. I serve as a member of the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ; soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024b ) , a community-led network that connects misophonia researchers with people who have lived experience of the condition. soQuiet’s network was created in part because, for years, misophonia research happened to people with misophonia rather than with them; this asymmetry is common in disability research and is one that ASSETS has long worked to interrupt ( Spiel et al., 2020 ; Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Mankoff et al., 2010 ; Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) . My positionality is therefore not a methodological footnote: it is the reason this report exists. This experience report makes three contributions to the ASSETS community. First , I extend the conversation on trauma-informed design (TID) ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) by foregrounding two harms that TID has tended to treat as separable. Sensory trauma is the recurring, design-mediated harm of unavoidable exposure to audiovisual content one’s body cannot tolerate. Epistemic trauma is the cumulative harm of having one’s first-person account of that exposure systematically disbelieved ( Stinnett, 2018 ; Mohamed, 2024 ) . For misophones, these are not two stories but one: the sounds hurt, and the dismissal that follows hurts again. I also position TID as an extension of Universal Design, arguing that the curb-cut logic applies: sensory and recognition features that support misophones produce platforms more usable for everyone. Second , drawing on a re-reading of 16 semi-structured interviews with people who live with misophonia ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) , I show that the platforms misophones turn to for validation (closed Facebook groups, moderated subreddits, gated Discord servers) can themselves reproduce epistemic dismissal when a small number of moderators decide whose experiences count as legitimate. This complicates a finding from prior work that closed, moderated communities are simply “safer” alternatives to open ones ( Ammari et al., 2019 ; Andalibi, 2019 ) ; for our participants, the same gating that screened out hostile users also screened out members whose lived experience contradicted the moderator’s preferred theory of the condition. Third , I reflect on what it has been like, as a researcher, to interview people about an experience I share. The interviews surfaced not only my participants’ epistemic wounds but also some of my own.

sections.heading: 2.1. Trauma-Informed Design in HCI
sections.text: Trauma-informed approaches in HCI build on the SAMHSA framework’s emphasis on safety, trustworthiness, peer support, collaboration, empowerment, and attention to cultural and historical context. Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2022 ) brought these principles into computing through trauma-informed computing , arguing that designers should anticipate that users may carry trauma and design systems that minimize re-traumatization. Scott et al. ( Scott et al., 2023 ) extended this lens to social media, presenting the six SAMHSA principles as “sensitizing concepts” rather than a checklist, and including the physical environment in which trauma occurs (citing supportive-housing work designing calming colors, materials, and lighting). Randazzo et al. ( Randazzo et al., 2023 ) push the field further by treating TID as fundamentally collaborative: indicators, metrics, and guidelines should be developed with affected users, clinicians, and practitioners rather than handed down from designers. Related work has examined content warnings, opt-in disclosure, and supportive moderation as ways to soften the platform’s impact on users carrying difficult histories ( Andalibi et al., 2016 ; Andalibi, 2017 ; Andalibi, 2019 ; Andalibi and Forte, 2018 ; Randazzo and Ammari, 2023 ) . It is useful to position TID, conceptually, as an under-theorized extension of Universal Design. Where Universal Design removes physical and sensory barriers to participation, TID addresses the affective and cognitive conditions that determine whether people can engage at all. The curb-cut effect is instructive: sidewalk curb cuts were designed for wheelchair users but came to benefit people who were never the intended beneficiaries, including parents with strollers, delivery workers, cyclists, and travelers with luggage ( Mankoff et al., 2010 ) . TID has the same logic. Design choices that reduce re-traumatization, build in user control, and lower the cognitive cost of participation help not only trauma survivors but everyone. This report argues that the curb-cut benefits of TID have not yet been claimed for sensory-sensitive users, and that, when they are, they will be felt well beyond that population. What the existing TID literature shares, however, is a focus on the content flowing through platforms and on whether users have controls to manage exposure to it. Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2022 ) note that trauma-informed safety includes physical conditions like “keeping noise levels low”; Scott et al. ( Scott et al., 2023 ) note that physical safety includes wall colors, lighting, and “being attentive to signs of discomfort.” But in both, the sensory environment is framed as a relatively static stage on which content-mediated harms happen, rather than as itself the harm. For embodied and contested conditions like misophonia, that framing under-specifies what trauma-informed design actually has to do.

sections.heading: 2.2. The Sensory Surface as a Site of Ongoing Trauma
sections.text: My prior work on misophonia and technology non-use ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) surfaces audiovisual challenges that are not edge cases but constitutive of how mainstream platforms work. TikTok’s For-You algorithm surfaces ASMR (deliberately triggering tapping, scratching, whispering) as “relaxing” content; Instagram and YouTube auto-play sounds; Zoom and Discord present a single shared audio mix in which a colleague’s chewing or pen-clicking sits at the same volume as their speech; and eating on camera, atypical in person, has become a normal video-meeting behavior. For someone with misophonia, these are not background design choices: they are recurring exposures to material the body responds to with anger, panic, or fight-or-flight ( Swedo et al., 2022 ; Jaswal et al., 2021 ) . Visual triggers (misokinesia) compound this; muting the audio does not silence the sight of someone chewing or fidgeting on screen. This pattern sits awkwardly inside the dominant TID framing. Treating trauma only as a carried-in history misses that, for sensory-sensitive users, the platform’s audiovisual surface is itself the re-traumatizing event: each unmuted call, each algorithmically surfaced ASMR clip, each unannounced mukbang 1 1 1 A video in which a host consumes large amounts of food while interacting with their audience. on the For-You page is an instance of harm produced by the system, not merely passing through it. Earlier accessibility work ( Race et al., 2021 ; Zolyomi and Snyder, 2021 ; Poulsen et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2021 ) charted some of the relevant vocabulary (sound duration, wavelength, and intensity; customizable sensory environments; sensory accommodation in remote work) and recent neurodivergent-design scholarship has pushed it further ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Sabinson, 2025a ; Sabinson, 2025b ; Baillargeon et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Nevsky et al., 2025 ) . Reading TID through this material reframes Chen et al.’s “noise levels” and Scott et al.’s “calming colors” not as a footnote but as a core obligation: a trauma-informed platform for sensory-sensitive users would treat the audiovisual surface as a moderation domain on the same footing as content, with design strategies (disaggregated audiovisual control, real-time sensory filtering, sensory predictability, collaborative boundary negotiation, and visual trigger management ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) ) available to users by default rather than negotiated case by case.

sections.heading: 2.3. Epistemic Injustice and Epistemic Trauma
sections.text: Sensory harm is half the story. The other half is who is believed when they describe it. Fricker ( Fricker, 2007 ) introduced epistemic injustice to name a wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower. Two forms matter here: testimonial injustice , where a speaker is given less credibility than they are due, and hermeneutical injustice , where no shared interpretive framework is available for someone to make sense of their experience. Carel and Kidd ( Carel and Kidd, 2014 ; Carel and Kidd, 2017 ; Kidd and Carel, 2017 ) developed this lens for healthcare; Newbigging and Ridley ( Newbigging and Ridley, 2018 ) and McKinnon ( McKinnon, 2016 ) document the same pattern in mental health, and Bhakuni and Abimbola ( Bhakuni and Abimbola, 2021 ) extend it into global health. Misophonia is a particularly clear case: it has no DSM entry, no consensus biomarker, and only recently received a published consensus definition ( Swedo et al., 2022 ) . Misophones face hermeneutical injustice (no widely shared vocabulary) and testimonial injustice (accounts doubted or pathologized) at the same time. The cumulative effect is what Stinnett ( Stinnett, 2018 ) names epistemic trauma : “after so [many] repeated instances of silencing, she begins to doubt her own experiences…and eventually no longer feels comfortable sharing” ( Stinnett, 2018 , p. 45–46) . Mohamed ( Mohamed, 2024 ) notes that this trauma can be transmitted, affecting both the person sharing and the professional, or the researcher, receiving. For HCI, the consequence is that two TID questions need to be asked together: whose body is the platform’s audiovisual surface designed for? , and whose account of that surface is the platform structured to take seriously? The structural version of the second question is one ASSETS already foregrounds: Spiel et al. ( Spiel et al., 2020 ) insist that “nothing about us” should be done “without us”; Hofmann et al. ( Hofmann et al., 2020 ) and Mack et al. ( Mack et al., 2021 ) interrogate which lived experiences accessibility research is built on; Bennett and Rosner ( Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) argue that empathy without lived expertise can mask whose authority is being centered.

sections.heading: 3. Approach
sections.text: This experience report is a re-reading of an earlier paper ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) , a qualitative analysis of 16 semi-structured interviews with U.S.-based adults who live with misophonia, recruited through online misophonia communities. The full study design, participant table, recruitment, and analytic procedure are reported there. Here I draw on three intertwined sources: my own lived experience with misophonia, my work with the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ) , and a return to those 16 transcripts with two specific lenses. The first lens asks where participants described specific platform surfaces (auto-playing audio, ASMR feeds, video-call audio mixes, eating on camera) producing distress that platform features could not let them manage. The second asks where they described being unable to share that experience, or described specific platform structures (moderation, gated access, single-moderator authority) that made it harder rather than easier to be believed. I read those passages alongside the literature on epistemic injustice ( Fricker, 2007 ; Carel and Kidd, 2014 ; Stinnett, 2018 ; Mohamed, 2024 ) and on trauma-informed design ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) . The findings below are not new fieldwork. They are a reflective re-reading, a style consistent with prior ASSETS work that treats researcher positionality as an analytic resource rather than a confound ( Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Branham and Kane, 2015 ) . I share many of the triggers participants described. I have had clinicians look at me blankly when I named the condition, and I have left online communities I once relied on. Working with the soQuiet network has also made plain to me that “misophonia community” is not a monolith: it is a fragile, internally contested space, and the boundaries of who is a credible speaker inside it are themselves under negotiation.

sections.heading: 4. What Participants Could Not Manage, and What They Could Not Share
sections.text: Across the 16 interviews, four patterns stood out. The first turns on platform surfaces that participants could not opt out of without leaving the platform; the second and third turn on whose account is treated as legitimate; the fourth on how the platform’s identity and feedback affordances shape who speaks at all.

sections.heading: 4.1. Sensory Trauma in Platform Surfaces
sections.text: Participants described the audiovisual fabric of mainstream platforms as a site of recurring distress, not background. Kathleen and Cindy each described TikTok as a platform whose value proposition (audio-synchronized content delivered without sensory pre-screening) put them in an impossible position: Kathleen had a “love-hate” relationship with the platform because the algorithm kept surfacing ASMR she could not tolerate, while Cindy left the platform altogether because she could not watch the videos without sound and watching with sound meant constant exposure ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . Read against TID, what is striking is that neither account is a content-moderation problem in the standard sense: the sounds involved are not abusive but ASMR clips and mukbangs delivered as “relaxing” content. Video conferencing produced a different but related pattern. Rhys characterized Zoom as “so auditory” that long sessions (her examples were three-hour Discord D&D nights and Zoom team meetings) became sustained trigger exposure she could only blunt with the platform’s coarse mute-all/hear-all controls. Nathan described eating on camera as both an audio and a visual trigger: “I’m not fond of people eating on Zoom…I don’t want to hear it. And I don’t want to watch it…if hearing them is maybe a nine, you know, seeing it as, like a two or three.” Amelia reported confronting a music teacher who ate during lessons, “feel[ing] weird telling her this” because the disclosure made her, not the eating, the social problem. Participants consistently described the binary mute/unmute structure of these platforms as itself the issue: there was no per-participant volume, no separation of speech from ambient sound, no way to blur a single video feed without affecting the rest ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . What makes these accounts traumatizing is their unannounced, unfilterable, recurring delivery into bodies that respond to them with fight-or-flight. The Race et al. ( Race et al., 2021 ) auditory design recommendations (sound duration, wavelength, intensity, recognizability) and the Jiang et al. ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) ADHD-inclusive principles (designs adapt to varying focus, multisensory flexibility, participatory involvement) point at the right vocabulary. What is needed at the platform level is to treat that vocabulary as part of trauma-informed design’s “safety” principle, not as a separate accessibility silo.

sections.heading: 4.2. “Are You Lying?”: Disbelief in Clinical and Family Settings
sections.text: Participants repeatedly described being disbelieved when they tried to name their experience. Evelyn told us she felt she had to come to interactions armed with research articles in order to be taken seriously; the everyday disbelief she encountered (“Are you lying?”) made her feel “unimportant” ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . That phrasing is, I think, an exact description of testimonial injustice ( Fricker, 2007 ) : not that one’s testimony is rebutted on the merits, but that one is not granted standing as a knower of one’s own life. Kathleen, who has a master’s in psychology and works as an organizational psychologist, described seeing three or four specialists and several general clinicians without finding anyone who could help. The structural absence of credible interlocutors is exhausting in itself, and substantial professional literacy does not protect against it ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . Lydia, looking back on years before she had a name for what she was experiencing, described what hermeneutical injustice feels like from inside: “I, like, pretty much thought I was insane from…the whole time, really.” Lydia and others also described family members who, after disclosure, made the trigger sounds on purpose. As one example, a relative would open a bag of chips with “oh, is this gonna be too loud for you?” The pattern (disclosure followed by deliberate triggering) is a specific weaponization of the epistemic position the discloser was trying to claim. The harm is not only that recognition fails; it is that the discloser is repeatedly required to prove themselves , against the default assumption that they are exaggerating.

sections.heading: 4.3. When the Online Community Becomes a Gated Community
sections.text: For people who do not get recognition from clinicians or family, online community is often the first place they feel believed. But the platforms participants used to reach those communities are not neutral: they impose structures of access that decide whose accounts get heard. Several participants described private, moderator-gated groups as both refuge and barrier. Lola had joined a private Facebook misophonia group years earlier and almost forgotten about it; the gate was both Facebook’s own (the platform was “not as accessible” to her) and the persistent expectation that sharing would go badly. Justine described herself as “too much of a private person…Sometimes I write [a comment] down…and then I’ll delete it. I just don’t want to be out there online.” Chuck named the trade-off in moderation gating directly: gated subreddits screen out trolls, but they also screen out the very people who might most benefit, those unwilling to apply to a group whose contents they cannot see in advance ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . Ashley’s account, more than any other in the corpus, pushed me toward this report’s framing. She had joined a closed Facebook group run by a single physician-moderator and initially valued it. When she brought in research arguing that misophonia has psychological and neurological dimensions alongside the auditory (a position consistent with the broader literature ( Swedo et al., 2022 ; Cavanna and Seri, 2015 ; Potgieter et al., 2019 ; Jaswal et al., 2021 ; Schröder et al., 2013 ; Taylor, 2017 ) ) and named her own visual triggers as embodied evidence, the moderator rejected the psychological framing outright and banned her, in Ashley’s words, “just for asserting that.” Ashley was not removed for harassment. She was removed for using her own embodied evidence (her visual triggers, her psychological responses) to push back on the moderator’s theory. The platform feature that gave the moderator authority to keep harassers out also gave her authority to keep contradictory lived experience out. From inside the group, the moderator’s theory looked like settled fact; from outside, what had happened was that a single gatekeeper had used the platform’s moderation affordances to enforce her interpretive frame against members whose first-person accounts did not fit. This is the structural shape of testimonial injustice, implemented in code. Ashley described a second harm: harassment that followed her across subreddits. After a disagreement on an unrelated subreddit, another user pulled her misophonia posts forward and used them against her, “denigrating me for, you know, this misophonia that I have and like, you’re crazy.” She reported the user to multiple moderation teams, including the misophonia subreddit’s. “Nobody did anything. Nobody cared at all,” she said. The first incident showed her what concentrated moderator authority does when it goes wrong; the second showed her what diffuse moderator authority does when it does nothing at all.

sections.heading: 4.4. Anonymity, Asymmetric Feedback, and Self-Censorship
sections.text: A quieter pattern runs through the transcripts: people whose willingness to share is shaped by the platform’s identity and feedback affordances. Several participants named anonymity as the precondition for sharing at all. Kathleen described “a lot of shame” around the condition and explained why Reddit was the only space she used for it: “Reddit is truly the one place where it’s completely anonymous…that feels very safe.” Vlad framed the calculus more sharply. In non-anonymous spaces, he said, “best case scenario, people are not going to be able to relate, and worst case scenario, they’ll be dismissive, or even put it on you.” Lola, who has an Instagram account, will not post about misophonia by name; the gate, again, is identifiability rather than reach. What Reddit’s pseudonymous architecture supplies for these participants is not anonymity-as-privacy in the usual sense, but anonymity-as-credibility-protection : a way to speak without having one’s standing on the topic adjudicated against an offline identity. Reddit’s voting affordances cut the other way. Kendra valued misophonia subreddits as “a realm that’s not just going to downvote me into oblivion”; Kathleen, who replies to younger users’ posts, observed that “people don’t really reply back that often…they just kind of like upvote the posts.” The platform’s primary feedback channel is a one-bit signal that a post is acceptable, not a substantive sign that the experience behind it has been recognized. A third response is outright withholding. Justine writes comments and deletes them. Evelyn “mostly go[es] on there just to like, be validated…I don’t make any posts myself.” Kathleen, by her own description, reads everything and posts almost nothing of her own. Many participants combined active community membership with very low public visibility: they read, they upvoted, they took screenshots, but they did not author. In Stinnett’s ( Stinnett, 2018 ) language, repeated silencing leads people to doubt their own experiences and “eventually no longer feel…comfortable sharing.” Self-censorship is not a personality trait. It is what epistemic trauma looks like as a long-run user-behavior pattern, shaped by the identity and feedback affordances the platform makes available.

sections.heading: 4.5. New Reflections
sections.text: The original paper ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) read these transcripts through platform affordances and selective domestication ( Salovaara et al., 2011 ; Sørensen, 2006 ; Gorm and Shklovski, 2019 ; Baumer et al., 2013 ; Baumer et al., 2014 ) , producing a five-principle design framework that still holds. What it underweighted is how cleanly those principles sit inside trauma-informed design. Two reframings emerge. (1) Sensory accessibility is trauma-informed safety. What Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2022 ) note in passing as “keeping noise levels low” is, for sensory-sensitive users, the central content of the safety principle online; ASMR auto-play and unfilterable Zoom audio are standing TID violations, not edge-case accessibility issues. (2) Recognition is itself a platform feature. Whether a user is believed when they describe their condition is shaped by who is granted moderation authority and what evidence counts, something invisible in standard affordance analyses, which treat moderation as backdrop. Closed, moderated communities, often valorized as “safer” ( Ammari et al., 2019 ; Andalibi, 2019 ) , can institutionalize a single moderator’s theory at the expense of members whose lived experience contradicts it.

sections.heading: 5. Reflection: Researching What You Live With
sections.text: When Ashley described being kicked out of a group for naming her visual triggers, I recognized her account immediately, because I have visual triggers, and because I have argued for the legitimacy of those triggers in spaces where the dominant theory of misophonia treats it as purely auditory. When Kathleen described seeing four specialists and finding none who could help, I recognized that too. The interviews were not abstractly painful. They were specifically painful in the sense Mohamed ( Mohamed, 2024 ) describes: epistemic trauma can pass between the person sharing and the person receiving. The same is true on the sensory side. I was the researcher, but I was also the person who has had to stop a Zoom call because of someone else’s lunch. Two practical commitments followed. On disclosure: I named my misophonia when relevant but tried not to use it as a credentialing move; I wrote detailed memos after each interview about agreements, surprises, and divergences, treating my reactions as data rather than background, consistent with autoethnographic and autobiographical-design traditions in HCI ( Branham and Kane, 2015 ; Sabinson, 2025b ) . On accountability: my affiliation with the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ) means the people whose experiences I write about are people I will see at workshops and on calls. The arguments here have to be defensible to the people they describe. ASSETS has long been a venue where this kind of accountability is taken seriously ( Spiel et al., 2020 ; Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) .

sections.heading: 6. Implications for the ASSETS Community
sections.text: Three implications follow. None is settled; all are offered for discussion.

sections.heading: 1. Make sensory and epistemic harm jointly visible inside trauma-informed design.
sections.text: TID conversations ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) have largely treated trauma as carried-in history that platforms should not reactivate, with the sensory environment treated as a static stage. For embodied and contested conditions like misophonia, trauma is also being produced in real time by the audiovisual surface and by the interactions in which the person’s account of their own body is doubted. Designs that take this seriously should ask three questions together: does this surface re-expose users to triggering content; does the platform let sensory-sensitive users participate without an all-or-nothing choice between meaningful presence and physiological distress; and does this surface treat users as credible knowers of their own condition, or does it require them to keep proving themselves? Concretely, this means treating disaggregated audiovisual control, real-time sensory filtering, sensory predictability, collaborative boundary negotiation, and visual trigger management ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) as TID safety features rather than accessibility add-ons; and pairing them with explicit moderation policies that name first-person accounts as a recognized form of evidence, user-controlled disclosure tools that do not require an authoritative diagnostic label, anonymity-preserving identity affordances so that disclosure does not turn the discloser’s offline standing into an evidentiary problem, and recognition mechanisms (badges, peer endorsements, substantive replies rather than only votes) that distribute credibility across community members. By the curb-cut logic of Section 2 , these are not niche accommodations: per-participant volume, ASMR-aware feed controls, mute-eating-only options, and recognition mechanisms that distribute credibility help misophones first, but they help anyone in a noisy household, anyone in back-to-back meetings, anyone whose lived experience is contested, and anyone whose attention budget is finite.

sections.heading: 2. Treat moderation architecture as an accessibility feature.
sections.text: ASSETS researchers already treat captioning, alt text, and contrast as accessibility features. The data suggest that moderation architecture (who can ban, who can pin, whose post is removed and on what grounds) is also an accessibility feature for people whose condition is contested. Concentrated moderator authority can institutionalize a single theory of the condition at the cost of members whose embodied experience contradicts it. Distributed approaches, such as rotating moderators, multi-moderator consensus for membership decisions, transparent appeals processes, and a separation of harassment-removal from interpretive-disagreement-removal, are accessibility infrastructure, not just governance ( Scott et al., 2023 ; Andalibi, 2017 ; Andalibi, 2019 ; Ammari et al., 2019 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) .

sections.heading: 3. Make space for researchers with the conditions they study, including the structures that protect them.
sections.text: The accessibility research community has come a long way on lived expertise ( Spiel et al., 2020 ; Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) . What still needs more explicit support is the labor of researchers who carry the conditions they study into the research itself, including emotional and sensory labor that does not fit neatly into project budgets. Concrete steps include protecting and celebrating autoethnographic and experience-report tracks; funding peer accountability structures like soQuiet’s research network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ) ; and treating researcher positionality not as confessional disclosure at the start of a paper but as an analytic resource that runs through it.

sections.heading: 7. Limitations
sections.text: This report is not a generalizable empirical study. The 16 interviews it draws on are a small, U.S.-based, predominantly white, predominantly female sample, recruited through online misophonia communities; participants who never found those communities, or who left them and never returned, are by construction underrepresented. The re-reading I have done is mine; another researcher reading the same transcripts (particularly one without misophonia, or with a different relationship to the soQuiet research network) would surface different patterns. Future work, including participatory work led by misophones, should test, complicate, and where necessary contradict what I have argued here.

sections.heading: 8. Conclusion
sections.text: For people who live with misophonia, the everyday harm is not only the sounds. It is also the dismissal that follows when one tries to name them. Trauma-informed design has given the HCI community a vocabulary for taking carried-in trauma seriously ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) . This experience report argues that, for embodied and contested conditions, that vocabulary needs to do two more things at once: take the platform’s audiovisual surface seriously as an ongoing site of sensory trauma, and take the platform’s moderation architecture seriously as an ongoing site of epistemic trauma. For the ASSETS community, doing so also means continuing to make room for researchers who write from inside the conditions they study, and for the community structures that hold that work accountable.

This experience report reflects on researching misophonia as someone who lives with it. Misophonia is an aversive response to everyday sounds (chewing, sniffling, pen clicking) and, for many of us, to associated visual cues (misokinesia). It is poorly recognized clinically and socially. People with misophonia are routinely disbelieved, and they live inside platform surfaces (auto-playing audio, algorithmic ASMR, normalized eating on camera) that turn the sensory environment itself into recurring distress. This report is a re-reading of a prior qualitative study of 16 semi-structured interviews with misophones ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) , conducted in dialogue with my lived experience and my role in the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network. I extend the trauma-informed design (TID) conversation ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) in two ways. First, TID must treat embodied, contested conditions as sources of both sensory and epistemic harm: ongoing trauma produced by the audiovisual surface and by repeated dismissal of users’ accounts of their bodies. Second, the closed groups and moderated subreddits participants relied on can reproduce that dismissal when a few moderators decide whose experiences count. I close with implications for ASSETS. Keywords: misophonia, misokinesia, trauma-informed design, sensory trauma, epistemic trauma, online communities, content moderation, sensory accessibility, autoethnography, lived experience, neurodivergence 1. Introduction and Positionality I write this report as someone who lives with misophonia and as a researcher who studies how design can support people whose experiences are routinely disbelieved. Misophonia is an aversive, often involuntary response to specific everyday sounds (chewing, slurping, sniffling, tongue clicking, pen clicking, keyboard typing, joint cracking) and, for many of us, to the visual cues that accompany them, a co-occurring sensitivity sometimes called misokinesia ( Jaswal et al., 2021 ) . Recent consensus work defines misophonia as a distinct disorder of decreased tolerance to specific sounds ( Swedo et al., 2022 ) , but it has no DSM entry and no settled clinical home ( Cavanna and Seri, 2015 ; Schröder et al., 2013 ; Taylor, 2017 ; Potgieter et al., 2019 ) . People who live with it spend extraordinary effort just to be believed , and, in parallel, extraordinary effort to make ordinary platform surfaces survivable. I serve as a member of the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ; soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024b ) , a community-led network that connects misophonia researchers with people who have lived experience of the condition. soQuiet’s network was created in part because, for years, misophonia research happened to people with misophonia rather than with them; this asymmetry is common in disability research and is one that ASSETS has long worked to interrupt ( Spiel et al., 2020 ; Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Mankoff et al., 2010 ; Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) . My positionality is therefore not a methodological footnote: it is the reason this report exists. This experience report makes three contributions to the ASSETS community. First , I extend the conversation on trauma-informed design (TID) ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) by foregrounding two harms that TID has tended to treat as separable. Sensory trauma is the recurring, design-mediated harm of unavoidable exposure to audiovisual content one’s body cannot tolerate. Epistemic trauma is the cumulative harm of having one’s first-person account of that exposure systematically disbelieved ( Stinnett, 2018 ; Mohamed, 2024 ) . For misophones, these are not two stories but one: the sounds hurt, and the dismissal that follows hurts again. I also position TID as an extension of Universal Design, arguing that the curb-cut logic applies: sensory and recognition features that support misophones produce platforms more usable for everyone. Second , drawing on a re-reading of 16 semi-structured interviews with people who live with misophonia ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) , I show that the platforms misophones turn to for validation (closed Facebook groups, moderated subreddits, gated Discord servers) can themselves reproduce epistemic dismissal when a small number of moderators decide whose experiences count as legitimate. This complicates a finding from prior work that closed, moderated communities are simply “safer” alternatives to open ones ( Ammari et al., 2019 ; Andalibi, 2019 ) ; for our participants, the same gating that screened out hostile users also screened out members whose lived experience contradicted the moderator’s preferred theory of the condition. Third , I reflect on what it has been like, as a researcher, to interview people about an experience I share. The interviews surfaced not only my participants’ epistemic wounds but also some of my own. 2. Background: Trauma-Informed Design Meets Sensory Trauma 2.1. Trauma-Informed Design in HCI Trauma-informed approaches in HCI build on the SAMHSA framework’s emphasis on safety, trustworthiness, peer support, collaboration, empowerment, and attention to cultural and historical context. Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2022 ) brought these principles into computing through trauma-informed computing , arguing that designers should anticipate that users may carry trauma and design systems that minimize re-traumatization. Scott et al. ( Scott et al., 2023 ) extended this lens to social media, presenting the six SAMHSA principles as “sensitizing concepts” rather than a checklist, and including the physical environment in which trauma occurs (citing supportive-housing work designing calming colors, materials, and lighting). Randazzo et al. ( Randazzo et al., 2023 ) push the field further by treating TID as fundamentally collaborative: indicators, metrics, and guidelines should be developed with affected users, clinicians, and practitioners rather than handed down from designers. Related work has examined content warnings, opt-in disclosure, and supportive moderation as ways to soften the platform’s impact on users carrying difficult histories ( Andalibi et al., 2016 ; Andalibi, 2017 ; Andalibi, 2019 ; Andalibi and Forte, 2018 ; Randazzo and Ammari, 2023 ) . It is useful to position TID, conceptually, as an under-theorized extension of Universal Design. Where Universal Design removes physical and sensory barriers to participation, TID addresses the affective and cognitive conditions that determine whether people can engage at all. The curb-cut effect is instructive: sidewalk curb cuts were designed for wheelchair users but came to benefit people who were never the intended beneficiaries, including parents with strollers, delivery workers, cyclists, and travelers with luggage ( Mankoff et al., 2010 ) . TID has the same logic. Design choices that reduce re-traumatization, build in user control, and lower the cognitive cost of participation help not only trauma survivors but everyone. This report argues that the curb-cut benefits of TID have not yet been claimed for sensory-sensitive users, and that, when they are, they will be felt well beyond that population. What the existing TID literature shares, however, is a focus on the content flowing through platforms and on whether users have controls to manage exposure to it. Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2022 ) note that trauma-informed safety includes physical conditions like “keeping noise levels low”; Scott et al. ( Scott et al., 2023 ) note that physical safety includes wall colors, lighting, and “being attentive to signs of discomfort.” But in both, the sensory environment is framed as a relatively static stage on which content-mediated harms happen, rather than as itself the harm. For embodied and contested conditions like misophonia, that framing under-specifies what trauma-informed design actually has to do. 2.2. The Sensory Surface as a Site of Ongoing Trauma My prior work on misophonia and technology non-use ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) surfaces audiovisual challenges that are not edge cases but constitutive of how mainstream platforms work. TikTok’s For-You algorithm surfaces ASMR (deliberately triggering tapping, scratching, whispering) as “relaxing” content; Instagram and YouTube auto-play sounds; Zoom and Discord present a single shared audio mix in which a colleague’s chewing or pen-clicking sits at the same volume as their speech; and eating on camera, atypical in person, has become a normal video-meeting behavior. For someone with misophonia, these are not background design choices: they are recurring exposures to material the body responds to with anger, panic, or fight-or-flight ( Swedo et al., 2022 ; Jaswal et al., 2021 ) . Visual triggers (misokinesia) compound this; muting the audio does not silence the sight of someone chewing or fidgeting on screen. This pattern sits awkwardly inside the dominant TID framing. Treating trauma only as a carried-in history misses that, for sensory-sensitive users, the platform’s audiovisual surface is itself the re-traumatizing event: each unmuted call, each algorithmically surfaced ASMR clip, each unannounced mukbang 1 1 1 A video in which a host consumes large amounts of food while interacting with their audience. on the For-You page is an instance of harm produced by the system, not merely passing through it. Earlier accessibility work ( Race et al., 2021 ; Zolyomi and Snyder, 2021 ; Poulsen et al., 2024 ; Das et al., 2021 ) charted some of the relevant vocabulary (sound duration, wavelength, and intensity; customizable sensory environments; sensory accommodation in remote work) and recent neurodivergent-design scholarship has pushed it further ( Jiang et al., 2025 ; Sabinson, 2025a ; Sabinson, 2025b ; Baillargeon et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2024 ; Nevsky et al., 2025 ) . Reading TID through this material reframes Chen et al.’s “noise levels” and Scott et al.’s “calming colors” not as a footnote but as a core obligation: a trauma-informed platform for sensory-sensitive users would treat the audiovisual surface as a moderation domain on the same footing as content, with design strategies (disaggregated audiovisual control, real-time sensory filtering, sensory predictability, collaborative boundary negotiation, and visual trigger management ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) ) available to users by default rather than negotiated case by case. 2.3. Epistemic Injustice and Epistemic Trauma Sensory harm is half the story. The other half is who is believed when they describe it. Fricker ( Fricker, 2007 ) introduced epistemic injustice to name a wrong done to someone in their capacity as a knower. Two forms matter here: testimonial injustice , where a speaker is given less credibility than they are due, and hermeneutical injustice , where no shared interpretive framework is available for someone to make sense of their experience. Carel and Kidd ( Carel and Kidd, 2014 ; Carel and Kidd, 2017 ; Kidd and Carel, 2017 ) developed this lens for healthcare; Newbigging and Ridley ( Newbigging and Ridley, 2018 ) and McKinnon ( McKinnon, 2016 ) document the same pattern in mental health, and Bhakuni and Abimbola ( Bhakuni and Abimbola, 2021 ) extend it into global health. Misophonia is a particularly clear case: it has no DSM entry, no consensus biomarker, and only recently received a published consensus definition ( Swedo et al., 2022 ) . Misophones face hermeneutical injustice (no widely shared vocabulary) and testimonial injustice (accounts doubted or pathologized) at the same time. The cumulative effect is what Stinnett ( Stinnett, 2018 ) names epistemic trauma : “after so [many] repeated instances of silencing, she begins to doubt her own experiences…and eventually no longer feels comfortable sharing” ( Stinnett, 2018 , p. 45–46) . Mohamed ( Mohamed, 2024 ) notes that this trauma can be transmitted, affecting both the person sharing and the professional, or the researcher, receiving. For HCI, the consequence is that two TID questions need to be asked together: whose body is the platform’s audiovisual surface designed for? , and whose account of that surface is the platform structured to take seriously? The structural version of the second question is one ASSETS already foregrounds: Spiel et al. ( Spiel et al., 2020 ) insist that “nothing about us” should be done “without us”; Hofmann et al. ( Hofmann et al., 2020 ) and Mack et al. ( Mack et al., 2021 ) interrogate which lived experiences accessibility research is built on; Bennett and Rosner ( Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) argue that empathy without lived expertise can mask whose authority is being centered. 3. Approach This experience report is a re-reading of an earlier paper ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) , a qualitative analysis of 16 semi-structured interviews with U.S.-based adults who live with misophonia, recruited through online misophonia communities. The full study design, participant table, recruitment, and analytic procedure are reported there. Here I draw on three intertwined sources: my own lived experience with misophonia, my work with the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ) , and a return to those 16 transcripts with two specific lenses. The first lens asks where participants described specific platform surfaces (auto-playing audio, ASMR feeds, video-call audio mixes, eating on camera) producing distress that platform features could not let them manage. The second asks where they described being unable to share that experience, or described specific platform structures (moderation, gated access, single-moderator authority) that made it harder rather than easier to be believed. I read those passages alongside the literature on epistemic injustice ( Fricker, 2007 ; Carel and Kidd, 2014 ; Stinnett, 2018 ; Mohamed, 2024 ) and on trauma-informed design ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) . The findings below are not new fieldwork. They are a reflective re-reading, a style consistent with prior ASSETS work that treats researcher positionality as an analytic resource rather than a confound ( Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Branham and Kane, 2015 ) . I share many of the triggers participants described. I have had clinicians look at me blankly when I named the condition, and I have left online communities I once relied on. Working with the soQuiet network has also made plain to me that “misophonia community” is not a monolith: it is a fragile, internally contested space, and the boundaries of who is a credible speaker inside it are themselves under negotiation. 4. What Participants Could Not Manage, and What They Could Not Share Across the 16 interviews, four patterns stood out. The first turns on platform surfaces that participants could not opt out of without leaving the platform; the second and third turn on whose account is treated as legitimate; the fourth on how the platform’s identity and feedback affordances shape who speaks at all. 4.1. Sensory Trauma in Platform Surfaces Participants described the audiovisual fabric of mainstream platforms as a site of recurring distress, not background. Kathleen and Cindy each described TikTok as a platform whose value proposition (audio-synchronized content delivered without sensory pre-screening) put them in an impossible position: Kathleen had a “love-hate” relationship with the platform because the algorithm kept surfacing ASMR she could not tolerate, while Cindy left the platform altogether because she could not watch the videos without sound and watching with sound meant constant exposure ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . Read against TID, what is striking is that neither account is a content-moderation problem in the standard sense: the sounds involved are not abusive but ASMR clips and mukbangs delivered as “relaxing” content. Video conferencing produced a different but related pattern. Rhys characterized Zoom as “so auditory” that long sessions (her examples were three-hour Discord D&D nights and Zoom team meetings) became sustained trigger exposure she could only blunt with the platform’s coarse mute-all/hear-all controls. Nathan described eating on camera as both an audio and a visual trigger: “I’m not fond of people eating on Zoom…I don’t want to hear it. And I don’t want to watch it…if hearing them is maybe a nine, you know, seeing it as, like a two or three.” Amelia reported confronting a music teacher who ate during lessons, “feel[ing] weird telling her this” because the disclosure made her, not the eating, the social problem. Participants consistently described the binary mute/unmute structure of these platforms as itself the issue: there was no per-participant volume, no separation of speech from ambient sound, no way to blur a single video feed without affecting the rest ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . What makes these accounts traumatizing is their unannounced, unfilterable, recurring delivery into bodies that respond to them with fight-or-flight. The Race et al. ( Race et al., 2021 ) auditory design recommendations (sound duration, wavelength, intensity, recognizability) and the Jiang et al. ( Jiang et al., 2025 ) ADHD-inclusive principles (designs adapt to varying focus, multisensory flexibility, participatory involvement) point at the right vocabulary. What is needed at the platform level is to treat that vocabulary as part of trauma-informed design’s “safety” principle, not as a separate accessibility silo. 4.2. “Are You Lying?”: Disbelief in Clinical and Family Settings Participants repeatedly described being disbelieved when they tried to name their experience. Evelyn told us she felt she had to come to interactions armed with research articles in order to be taken seriously; the everyday disbelief she encountered (“Are you lying?”) made her feel “unimportant” ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . That phrasing is, I think, an exact description of testimonial injustice ( Fricker, 2007 ) : not that one’s testimony is rebutted on the merits, but that one is not granted standing as a knower of one’s own life. Kathleen, who has a master’s in psychology and works as an organizational psychologist, described seeing three or four specialists and several general clinicians without finding anyone who could help. The structural absence of credible interlocutors is exhausting in itself, and substantial professional literacy does not protect against it ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . Lydia, looking back on years before she had a name for what she was experiencing, described what hermeneutical injustice feels like from inside: “I, like, pretty much thought I was insane from…the whole time, really.” Lydia and others also described family members who, after disclosure, made the trigger sounds on purpose. As one example, a relative would open a bag of chips with “oh, is this gonna be too loud for you?” The pattern (disclosure followed by deliberate triggering) is a specific weaponization of the epistemic position the discloser was trying to claim. The harm is not only that recognition fails; it is that the discloser is repeatedly required to prove themselves , against the default assumption that they are exaggerating. 4.3. When the Online Community Becomes a Gated Community For people who do not get recognition from clinicians or family, online community is often the first place they feel believed. But the platforms participants used to reach those communities are not neutral: they impose structures of access that decide whose accounts get heard. Several participants described private, moderator-gated groups as both refuge and barrier. Lola had joined a private Facebook misophonia group years earlier and almost forgotten about it; the gate was both Facebook’s own (the platform was “not as accessible” to her) and the persistent expectation that sharing would go badly. Justine described herself as “too much of a private person…Sometimes I write [a comment] down…and then I’ll delete it. I just don’t want to be out there online.” Chuck named the trade-off in moderation gating directly: gated subreddits screen out trolls, but they also screen out the very people who might most benefit, those unwilling to apply to a group whose contents they cannot see in advance ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) . Ashley’s account, more than any other in the corpus, pushed me toward this report’s framing. She had joined a closed Facebook group run by a single physician-moderator and initially valued it. When she brought in research arguing that misophonia has psychological and neurological dimensions alongside the auditory (a position consistent with the broader literature ( Swedo et al., 2022 ; Cavanna and Seri, 2015 ; Potgieter et al., 2019 ; Jaswal et al., 2021 ; Schröder et al., 2013 ; Taylor, 2017 ) ) and named her own visual triggers as embodied evidence, the moderator rejected the psychological framing outright and banned her, in Ashley’s words, “just for asserting that.” Ashley was not removed for harassment. She was removed for using her own embodied evidence (her visual triggers, her psychological responses) to push back on the moderator’s theory. The platform feature that gave the moderator authority to keep harassers out also gave her authority to keep contradictory lived experience out. From inside the group, the moderator’s theory looked like settled fact; from outside, what had happened was that a single gatekeeper had used the platform’s moderation affordances to enforce her interpretive frame against members whose first-person accounts did not fit. This is the structural shape of testimonial injustice, implemented in code. Ashley described a second harm: harassment that followed her across subreddits. After a disagreement on an unrelated subreddit, another user pulled her misophonia posts forward and used them against her, “denigrating me for, you know, this misophonia that I have and like, you’re crazy.” She reported the user to multiple moderation teams, including the misophonia subreddit’s. “Nobody did anything. Nobody cared at all,” she said. The first incident showed her what concentrated moderator authority does when it goes wrong; the second showed her what diffuse moderator authority does when it does nothing at all. 4.4. Anonymity, Asymmetric Feedback, and Self-Censorship A quieter pattern runs through the transcripts: people whose willingness to share is shaped by the platform’s identity and feedback affordances. Several participants named anonymity as the precondition for sharing at all. Kathleen described “a lot of shame” around the condition and explained why Reddit was the only space she used for it: “Reddit is truly the one place where it’s completely anonymous…that feels very safe.” Vlad framed the calculus more sharply. In non-anonymous spaces, he said, “best case scenario, people are not going to be able to relate, and worst case scenario, they’ll be dismissive, or even put it on you.” Lola, who has an Instagram account, will not post about misophonia by name; the gate, again, is identifiability rather than reach. What Reddit’s pseudonymous architecture supplies for these participants is not anonymity-as-privacy in the usual sense, but anonymity-as-credibility-protection : a way to speak without having one’s standing on the topic adjudicated against an offline identity. Reddit’s voting affordances cut the other way. Kendra valued misophonia subreddits as “a realm that’s not just going to downvote me into oblivion”; Kathleen, who replies to younger users’ posts, observed that “people don’t really reply back that often…they just kind of like upvote the posts.” The platform’s primary feedback channel is a one-bit signal that a post is acceptable, not a substantive sign that the experience behind it has been recognized. A third response is outright withholding. Justine writes comments and deletes them. Evelyn “mostly go[es] on there just to like, be validated…I don’t make any posts myself.” Kathleen, by her own description, reads everything and posts almost nothing of her own. Many participants combined active community membership with very low public visibility: they read, they upvoted, they took screenshots, but they did not author. In Stinnett’s ( Stinnett, 2018 ) language, repeated silencing leads people to doubt their own experiences and “eventually no longer feel…comfortable sharing.” Self-censorship is not a personality trait. It is what epistemic trauma looks like as a long-run user-behavior pattern, shaped by the identity and feedback affordances the platform makes available. 4.5. New Reflections The original paper ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) read these transcripts through platform affordances and selective domestication ( Salovaara et al., 2011 ; Sørensen, 2006 ; Gorm and Shklovski, 2019 ; Baumer et al., 2013 ; Baumer et al., 2014 ) , producing a five-principle design framework that still holds. What it underweighted is how cleanly those principles sit inside trauma-informed design. Two reframings emerge. (1) Sensory accessibility is trauma-informed safety. What Chen et al. ( Chen et al., 2022 ) note in passing as “keeping noise levels low” is, for sensory-sensitive users, the central content of the safety principle online; ASMR auto-play and unfilterable Zoom audio are standing TID violations, not edge-case accessibility issues. (2) Recognition is itself a platform feature. Whether a user is believed when they describe their condition is shaped by who is granted moderation authority and what evidence counts, something invisible in standard affordance analyses, which treat moderation as backdrop. Closed, moderated communities, often valorized as “safer” ( Ammari et al., 2019 ; Andalibi, 2019 ) , can institutionalize a single moderator’s theory at the expense of members whose lived experience contradicts it. 5. Reflection: Researching What You Live With When Ashley described being kicked out of a group for naming her visual triggers, I recognized her account immediately, because I have visual triggers, and because I have argued for the legitimacy of those triggers in spaces where the dominant theory of misophonia treats it as purely auditory. When Kathleen described seeing four specialists and finding none who could help, I recognized that too. The interviews were not abstractly painful. They were specifically painful in the sense Mohamed ( Mohamed, 2024 ) describes: epistemic trauma can pass between the person sharing and the person receiving. The same is true on the sensory side. I was the researcher, but I was also the person who has had to stop a Zoom call because of someone else’s lunch. Two practical commitments followed. On disclosure: I named my misophonia when relevant but tried not to use it as a credentialing move; I wrote detailed memos after each interview about agreements, surprises, and divergences, treating my reactions as data rather than background, consistent with autoethnographic and autobiographical-design traditions in HCI ( Branham and Kane, 2015 ; Sabinson, 2025b ) . On accountability: my affiliation with the soQuiet Misophonia Research Network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ) means the people whose experiences I write about are people I will see at workshops and on calls. The arguments here have to be defensible to the people they describe. ASSETS has long been a venue where this kind of accountability is taken seriously ( Spiel et al., 2020 ; Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) . 6. Implications for the ASSETS Community Three implications follow. None is settled; all are offered for discussion. 1. Make sensory and epistemic harm jointly visible inside trauma-informed design. TID conversations ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) have largely treated trauma as carried-in history that platforms should not reactivate, with the sensory environment treated as a static stage. For embodied and contested conditions like misophonia, trauma is also being produced in real time by the audiovisual surface and by the interactions in which the person’s account of their own body is doubted. Designs that take this seriously should ask three questions together: does this surface re-expose users to triggering content; does the platform let sensory-sensitive users participate without an all-or-nothing choice between meaningful presence and physiological distress; and does this surface treat users as credible knowers of their own condition, or does it require them to keep proving themselves? Concretely, this means treating disaggregated audiovisual control, real-time sensory filtering, sensory predictability, collaborative boundary negotiation, and visual trigger management ( Ammari and Gilgan, 2026 ) as TID safety features rather than accessibility add-ons; and pairing them with explicit moderation policies that name first-person accounts as a recognized form of evidence, user-controlled disclosure tools that do not require an authoritative diagnostic label, anonymity-preserving identity affordances so that disclosure does not turn the discloser’s offline standing into an evidentiary problem, and recognition mechanisms (badges, peer endorsements, substantive replies rather than only votes) that distribute credibility across community members. By the curb-cut logic of Section 2 , these are not niche accommodations: per-participant volume, ASMR-aware feed controls, mute-eating-only options, and recognition mechanisms that distribute credibility help misophones first, but they help anyone in a noisy household, anyone in back-to-back meetings, anyone whose lived experience is contested, and anyone whose attention budget is finite. 2. Treat moderation architecture as an accessibility feature. ASSETS researchers already treat captioning, alt text, and contrast as accessibility features. The data suggest that moderation architecture (who can ban, who can pin, whose post is removed and on what grounds) is also an accessibility feature for people whose condition is contested. Concentrated moderator authority can institutionalize a single theory of the condition at the cost of members whose embodied experience contradicts it. Distributed approaches, such as rotating moderators, multi-moderator consensus for membership decisions, transparent appeals processes, and a separation of harassment-removal from interpretive-disagreement-removal, are accessibility infrastructure, not just governance ( Scott et al., 2023 ; Andalibi, 2017 ; Andalibi, 2019 ; Ammari et al., 2019 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) . 3. Make space for researchers with the conditions they study, including the structures that protect them. The accessibility research community has come a long way on lived expertise ( Spiel et al., 2020 ; Hofmann et al., 2020 ; Mack et al., 2021 ; Bennett and Rosner, 2019 ) . What still needs more explicit support is the labor of researchers who carry the conditions they study into the research itself, including emotional and sensory labor that does not fit neatly into project budgets. Concrete steps include protecting and celebrating autoethnographic and experience-report tracks; funding peer accountability structures like soQuiet’s research network ( soQuiet Misophonia Advocacy, 2024a ) ; and treating researcher positionality not as confessional disclosure at the start of a paper but as an analytic resource that runs through it. 7. Limitations This report is not a generalizable empirical study. The 16 interviews it draws on are a small, U.S.-based, predominantly white, predominantly female sample, recruited through online misophonia communities; participants who never found those communities, or who left them and never returned, are by construction underrepresented. The re-reading I have done is mine; another researcher reading the same transcripts (particularly one without misophonia, or with a different relationship to the soQuiet research network) would surface different patterns. Future work, including participatory work led by misophones, should test, complicate, and where necessary contradict what I have argued here. 8. Conclusion For people who live with misophonia, the everyday harm is not only the sounds. It is also the dismissal that follows when one tries to name them. Trauma-informed design has given the HCI community a vocabulary for taking carried-in trauma seriously ( Chen et al., 2022 ; Scott et al., 2023 ; Randazzo et al., 2023 ) . This experience report argues that, for embodied and contested conditions, that vocabulary needs to do two more things at once: take the platform’s audiovisual surface seriously as an ongoing site of sensory trauma, and take the platform’s moderation architecture seriously as an ongoing site of epistemic trauma. For the ASSETS community, doing so also means continuing to make room for researchers who write from inside the conditions they study, and for the community structures that hold that work accountable.
